question: Once the personas walk a live browser and say DONE or NOT, who on the team actually turns that verdict into a design decision, and can anyone decline what the panel asks for?
When a usage limit cuts off a lane mid-work like you mentioned happened on September 7th, does that lane just stop, and how do you pick it back up?
Beyond the gate and flag, what stops an unattended agent run from merging broken code or overspending before you check on it?
The 65 percent right-card-in-top-3 figure on live lots comes from your own taps over five days — what's the sample size and confidence interval, and who else verified those calls?
For a product manager who isn't writing code or running worktrees, what's the concrete first thing to do differently on Monday?
You ran this mostly alone with full access to everything — what changes if a team of engineers, not one person, tries to run these lanes and gates?
What was the total cost of this project, including the Claude Max subscription itself, not just the nine dollars of metered spend?
How were the four persona briefs actually written — real device and job constraints, or just demographic labels with a task attached?
The language re-rank was found after your favorite idea failed the bar, on the same 201 photos — why report it as a shipped win rather than a lead needing a fresh held-out test?
Is about two in three on live auctions good enough to ship, and what's the next number you're actually trying to move?
Is the 'about 30 minutes a day' a timed measurement or your own estimate, and does it include the mornings spent reading results?
Dez's task time went from 30 seconds to 9, simulated — do you treat that as a usability number at all, or only as a proxy until a human confirms it?
You showed four different ways of scoring top-3 accuracy that don't agree — why pick the roughly two-in-three number as the one headline claim instead of reporting a range?
Once a gate passes, does the lane merge on its own, or do you still review the diff before it lands?
Is the full experiment ledger and decisions log in the public repo, or are some of the sources you cited private?
What exactly goes in the brief for a lane, and who writes the acceptance test when the fix isn't something you can score with a simple pass or fail?
Who sets the pass/fail bar for each gate, and how do you stop that number from being picked to guarantee the result you want?
When the scout was flapping, what did that actually look like to someone watching the stream — did you observe a real user's reaction, or only your own instrumented session?
What changed on the labeler review screen itself that cut your review time from three minutes to 20 to 30 seconds, and was that redesign tested on anyone besides you?
What does 'one tier up' actually mean in terms of which models you use for building versus reviewing?
After moving to a live browser and three widths, what specifically did the next panel catch before merge, beyond your own sense that things got better?
How did you land on caps like 8 calls, 60 seconds and $6 per run — is that trial and error, or is there a way to estimate it up front?
The persona panel said the build was done and it was unusable on your phone the next morning — what makes you confident the redesigned panel process wouldn't fail the same way again?
Is the persona panel meant to replace hands-on usability testing with real people, or only to feed and prioritize it — where's that line for you?
The starter kit covers finding the fix, testing the idea, and checking it's done — why is there nothing repeatable for deciding what to build first?
The persona panel said done and your own phone said otherwise the next morning — has that gap shown up again since you added the live-browser step?
Realistically how many lanes can you run at once before you're back to being the bottleneck reviewing all of them?
Before the phone test caught it, did anyone actually hold a device while building the UI, or was 'done' judged entirely on the fixed-size panel screens?
Your strongest model both writes the briefs and judges the results of the lanes it set up — what checks catch that model grading its own work favorably?
Is the forty-five-fork count and the claim that only two forks mattered a pre-registered tally, or a retrospective count made after you already knew which fixes worked?
About how many of the roughly hundred experiments ran fully unattended overnight versus needing you to check in or intervene?
For someone trying this next week, which single file in the starter kit should they open first?
A usage limit cut off three build lanes mid-work at one point — how would you plan capacity or budget around that at team scale?
Is the morning report with the calls only you can make something the gate assembles automatically, or do you have to write it yourself each night?
You used terms like top-3 and the box vote pretty quickly during the demo — can you spell out in plain terms what those mean?
For the crop-versus-vote decision that fixed misidentified cards, was that judged only by replaying recordings, or did a person watch it live on a real stream before it shipped?
